title: Historical Context and Classification Table
content: Sets up the complete solvability classification for alternating groups. The classification table shows: $A_0, A_1, A_2$ are trivial (order 1), $A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ is abelian, $A_4$ is solvable via the Klein four-group, and $A_n$ for $n \ge 5$ is simple and non-solvable. This is directly connected to the Abel-Ruffini theorem: the insolvability of $A_5$ is the group-theoretic reason why the general quintic equation has no radical solution.
mathContext: $A_n$ is solvable $\Leftrightarrow n \le 4$. The threshold is $n = 5$: $A_5$ (order 60) is the smallest non-abelian simple group. For $n \ge 5$, $A_n$ is simple, hence its derived series never reaches $\{e\}$.

title: Small Alternating Groups Are Solvable (n ≤ 4)
content: Proves solvability for $A_0$ through $A_4$. The trivial cases ($n \le 2$) use `inferInstance` since these are subsingleton groups. $A_3$ is handled by `isSolvable_of_comm` (abelian groups are solvable) with `decide` for commutativity. $A_4$ uses a two-step argument: first establish $S_4$ is solvable via `native_decide` on the derived series (length 3), then use that subgroups of solvable groups are solvable.
mathContext: $A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ (abelian, hence solvable). $A_4$ has composition series $A_4 \trianglerighteq V_4 \trianglerighteq \{e\}$ where $V_4 = \{\text{id}, (12)(34), (13)(24), (14)(23)\} \cong (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2$ and $A_4/V_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$. All factors are abelian, so $A_4$ is solvable. The Lean proof avoids computing this series directly, instead deducing solvability from the solvability of the ambient $S_4$.

title: Exact Sequence Argument: Aₙ Solvable Implies Sₙ Solvable
content: The key reduction: if $A_n$ is solvable, then $S_n$ is solvable. Uses the short exact sequence $1 \to A_n \xrightarrow{\iota} S_n \xrightarrow{\text{sign}} \mathbb{Z}^\times \to 1$, where $\ker(\text{sign}) = A_n$ and $\text{im}(\text{sign}) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ (solvable). Mathlib's `solvable_of_ker_le_range` gives: if both the kernel and quotient of a group extension are solvable, the group is solvable. Since $A_n$ is solvable (hypothesis) and $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ is solvable (abelian), $S_n$ is solvable.
mathContext: The short exact sequence $1 \to A_n \hookrightarrow S_n \xrightarrow{\text{sgn}} \{\pm 1\} \to 1$ has solvable kernel ($A_n$ by hypothesis) and solvable quotient ($\{\pm 1\} \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$). By the extension lemma for solvable groups, $S_n$ is solvable. The proof constructs the required membership: $x \in \ker(\text{sign})$ iff $x$ is an even permutation, i.e., $x \in A_n$.

title: Aₙ Not Solvable for n ≥ 5
content: Combines the two private lemmas: `sn_solvable_of_an_solvable` (the exact sequence reduction) and `sn_not_solvable` (Mathlib's `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable`). By contradiction: if $A_n$ were solvable for $n \ge 5$, then $S_n$ would be solvable, but Mathlib proves $\lnot\text{IsSolvable}(S_n)$ for $n \ge 5$ via the simplicity of $A_5$ and its embedding into $A_n$.
mathContext: $A_n$ solvable $\xRightarrow{\text{exact seq.}}$ $S_n$ solvable $\xRightarrow{\text{Mathlib}}$ contradiction for $n \ge 5$. Therefore $\lnot\text{IsSolvable}(A_n)$ for $n \ge 5$. The Mathlib proof of $S_n$ non-solvability ultimately relies on the simplicity of $A_5$: since $A_5$ has no non-trivial normal subgroups and is non-abelian, its derived series never terminates.

title: Main Theorem: Aₙ Solvable iff n ≤ 4
content: The complete classification `alternating_solvable_iff`: $\text{IsSolvable}(A_n) \leftrightarrow n \le 4$. The forward direction uses contradiction: if $A_n$ is solvable and $n > 4$, then $n \ge 5$ and `an_not_solvable_of_ge_five` gives a contradiction. The backward direction uses `interval_cases` to enumerate $n \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$ and applies the corresponding solvability theorem. This is a clean bidirectional proof combining all previous results.
mathContext: The theorem $A_n$ solvable $\Leftrightarrow n \le 4$ has the same threshold as $S_n$ solvable $\Leftrightarrow n \le 4$, because both are governed by the simplicity of $A_5$. In Galois theory terms: a polynomial of degree $n$ has Galois group $\subseteq S_n$, and if the Galois group is solvable, the roots are expressible by radicals. Since $S_5$ (and $A_5$) are not solvable, the general quintic is not solvable by radicals.

title: Named Corollaries and Sharp Threshold
content: Derives named instances for specific groups: `a5_not_solvable`, `a6_not_solvable`, `alternating_solvable_of_le_four`, `alternating_not_solvable_of_ge_five`. The `sharp_threshold` theorem explicitly states both sides of the boundary: $A_4$ IS solvable and $A_5$ is NOT. This makes the threshold maximally explicit and provides convenient API for downstream proofs.
mathContext: The sharp threshold at $n = 5$ reflects that $|A_5| = 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$, and $A_5$ is the unique simple group of order 60 (isomorphic to $\text{PSL}(2, 5) \cong \text{PSL}(2, 4) \cong$ the icosahedral rotation group). For $n \ge 5$, $A_5$ embeds in $A_n$ as the subgroup permuting only the first 5 elements.
